articles.title: Former Williams student gets 30 days in hidden camera case
articles.description: Maxwell Hall, a former wrestler at Williams College, pleaded guilty Wednesday to placing a hidden camera. PITTSFIELD -- A former Williams College student was sentenced to 30 days in jail for putting a hidden camera in a gym bathroom after pleading guilty Wednesday. Maxwell Hall, 23, was charged with 16 counts of photographing an unsuspecting nude person after a camera hidden in what appeared to be a phone charger was discovered in January 2025 in a single-stall bathroom in Lassell Fitness Center. Assistant District Attorney Rachael Eramo said the device was planted approximately six hours before being discovered. During that time, 16 people, all appearing to be college-aged, were recorded in varying states of undress. Out of the 16 recorded, 11 were identified by police with the help of the college. During a hearing last month in Berkshire Superior Court to discuss a plea deal, Eramo asked for 18 months of incarceration. She said in court that she understands that Hall does not have a criminal record, but the victims in the case feel violated, with several of the female victims still being afraid of using public bathrooms. "What Mr. Hall chose to do was so egregious," Eramo said in September. "He came out the gate pretty hot." During that hearing, defense lawyer Dan Kelly argued for two years of probation. He cited Hall's lack of criminal record and argued that Hall's obsessive-compulsive disorder affects his impulse control. During Wednesday's hearing, one of the victims spoke to the court over Zoom. She said she is disappointed with the 30-day sentence, saying that his actions were a "deliberate mass sexual assault." "Our dignity was robbed from us," she said. Eramo also read out a victim impact statement from a woman who was a senior at the college at the time. The former student wrote that she still cannot use public restrooms without fear. She characterized Hall's behavior as "actions of a sick individual." Judge James Manitsas, who appeared over Zoom, sentenced Hall to one year in the Berkshire House of Correction, with all but 30 days suspended. Hall will serve 30 days in jail, followed by one year of probation. The crime to which he pleaded guilty does not carry a requirement to register as a sex offender, but he will be evaluated as a sex offender as a condition of probation. He will continue psychological treatment and is ordered to not contact the named victims. Additionally, he is not allowed to possess surveillance equipment other than security devices for a residence.

pendingReview.title: Singapore national serviceman who allegedly trespassed into female toilet jumps from third-storey ledge, recovering in hospital
pendingReview.description: SINGAPORE, Oct 26 -- A full-time national serviceman (NSF) with the Singapore Police Force allegedly trespassed into a female toilet at the Police Training Command, where he is a staff member, before jumping from a third-storey ledge while being engaged by police officers. The 23-year-old was later arrested for criminal trespass and voyeurism. The police told AsiaOne they were alerted to the incident about 5.40am on October 19. Preliminary investigations found that the NSF had trespassed into a women's restroom. He was detained and police assistance was sought. While police officers were engaging him, the man suddenly ran away. He then made his way to the third storey of a nearby block and jumped off a ledge. The NSF was conscious when taken to the hospital, said the police, adding that he has been receiving treatment for his injuries. He was subsequently arrested. Police investigations are ongoing. -- AsiaOne

pendingReview.title: Claude Code Prompt Can Turn Your Laptop Into A Hidden Camera Detector For Hotel Rooms And Airbnbs, Sweeping Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Trackers, And Your Phone Before You Unpack
pendingReview.description: We've always had that looming fear that there's a hidden camera in a hotel room or Airbnb, recording your every move, and given that these are well concealed, it's difficult to determine their exact spot, unless you're willing to search every nook and cranny of the room. Fortunately, a single Claude Code prompt means you won't have to make that effort, because AI can help sweep a hotel room or Airbnb for hidden cameras, Bluetooth trackers, and phone spyware before you've unpacked. One user claims a friend used it to find a camera hidden behind a bathroom mirror in 90 seconds. Discovering the hidden camera using Claude Code takes five stages to complete The prompt shared by X user @Damir_Akaza casts Claude Code as a "check-in security assistant" and sets strict read-only rules. This virtual shield allows discovery and passive listening only, with no logins, default passwords, exploits, or touching devices that aren't the user's. The agent is also told to explain each command in one line before running it. The first step is a Wi-Fi scan, where the agent runs "arp-scan" and "nmap" to list every device on the guest network from MAC addresses. It then checks ports commonly used by cameras and flags vendors such as Hikvision and other brands, along with RTSP streaming ports. Also, Claude Code is explicitly told never to open a single stream. Next comes a Bluetooth scan. Using a short Python script built on the bleak library, Claude Code listens for 30 seconds every two minutes over a 10-minute window, logging manufacturer data, service UUIDs, and signal strength. The script then searches for Apple Find My, Tile, and Samsung SmartTag signatures, matching on payload and signal rather than MAC address since Bluetooth trackers rotate theirs. The post also says the third stage audits your phone using Amnesty International's open-source Mobile Verification Toolkit. If the hotel isolates guest devices on its network, the fourth stage has the agent walk you through a flashlight check of mirrors, vents, and angles facing the bed. The final stage builds a ranked table of suspicious findings, with suggested next steps ranging from asking for another room to calling the police. Of course, Claude Code has its limitations. For instance, a network scan can only find cameras on the network you're connected to, so if a device is recording to an SD card, running its own hotspot, or sitting behind guest isolation, it obviously won't show up. In short, a clean result doesn't necessarily mean that the hotel room or an Airbnb is safe to use, so be mindful of this. Claude Code certainly has its uses, but even on this occasion, we should treat it as a safeguard instead of a guarantee. Fortunately, the AI is capable of locating spyware and backdoors on Macs, not to mention hidden cryptominers, so it's more than useful in a multitude of cases.

pendingReview.title: Carer jailed after family uncovers theft using hidden camera
pendingReview.description: A carer who stole thousands worth of jewellery from an elderly and vulnerable client has been jailed for three years after the victim's family caught her red-handed using a hidden camera. Lara Jones, 50 from Kent in the UK, was sentenced on Friday, October 9, after being found guilty of three counts of burglary following a trial. The court heard that on November 26, 2025, Jones entered her client's bedroom at his home during her very first shift. Following her departure, the victim's family spotted an earring at the top of the stairs. When they went to return it to a bedroom jewellery box, they discovered multiple pieces of valuable jewellery were missing. Unsure but suspicious of the new carer, the family took quick-thinking action and installed hidden cameras inside the bedroom. When Jones returned for her second shift, the covert cameras captured her opening drawers, searching wardrobes, and pocketing jewellery worth a total of £8,000. On Wednesday, December 3, the victim's daughter alerted Surrey Police while her vulnerable father was alone in the house with Jones. Officers immediately attended the scene and arrested Jones on suspicion of burglary. A search revealed the stolen jewellery in her possession. Despite pleading not guilty, Jones was convicted by a jury. Along with a three-year prison sentence, she was ordered to pay a victim surcharge of £228. In a statement following the sentencing, the victim's family expressed the deep emotional toll of the crime: 'Having someone violate your trust in your own home, at a time when you are at your most vulnerable, is devastating. The emotional impact has been profound, and it has made an already difficult situation even harder. 'We are immensely grateful to Surrey Police and the Crown Prosecution Service for their dedication, compassion and determination in securing this conviction. Their support throughout has meant a great deal to our family, and we are relieved that justice has been served.'
